speechtext:
Motion No. 14
That Bill C-78, an act to provide for the payment of benefits to laid-off employees and to amend the Canada Labour Code, be amended in Clause 12 by adding immediately after line 29 at page 8 the following:
"(c) an employee shall be considered to have worked 1,000 hours in a year in each year for which he failed to work 1,000 hours because he was in receipt of a disability pension, sick benefits, workers compensation or was on leave of absence with the consent of the employer." and that the following paragraphs be renumbered accordingly.
Mr. Speaker, I want to speak specifically to Motion No. 13, if I may.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Motion No. 13 stands in the name of the Minister of Labour. I should like to draw that fact to the attention of the House.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I see no problem in that regard. Earlier today the Speaker ruled that Motions Nos. 13 and 14 could be debated together but voted on separately.

In fact I was quite prepared to concede that it stood in the name of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia); I would not want to claim credit for it. I should like to draw to the attention of the minister paragraph (b)(3) of Motion No. 13, which reads:
Notwithstanding Subsection (1), where an employee certified under Section 10 would be qualified under Subsection (1) to receive labour adjustment benefits but for the requirement set out in paragraph (l)(b), the commission may determine-
The word "may" is the word which concerns me. I should like the minister to think for a moment about the possible consequences of "may", given the qualification which is then set out in the clause. It continues:
-that the employee is qualified to receive labour adjustment benefits if he shows that he is in substantial compliance with the requirement and that he docs not meet such requirement by reason only of illness, disability, lay-off or any other good cause whatsoever.

February 15, 1982
Labour Adjustment Benefits
I suggest the minister should listen; I am not rising to speak because I like to listen to myself at 9.32 p.m.
That is a change.

I am rising to speak because 1 happen to think, despite the fact the hon. member for Brampton-Georgetown (Mr. McDermid) is intervening from his newfound front seat, which no doubt is temporary, that the minister might consider the consequences of the word "may". If an employee goes before the board and is able to prove that he would normally meet the requirements of the act for benefit, and if he were able to show that the only reason he was disentitled from receiving benefit was illness, disability or lay-off during the period under consideration, or any other good cause whatsoever, I contend that the word "may" ought not to be there. Surely the board shall find, in cases where it is proven to the satisfaction of the board that the employee would otherwise be entitled, except for illness, lay-off, disability or another cause which the board determines is a good cause, in favour of the employee. I think the employee is being put in double jeopardy. He must go before the board to try to prove, on the one hand, that there is good and justifiable reason why he should be eligible. On the other hand, having once proven it even to the satisfaction of the board, he must then await the board's determination as to whether or not it will accept the circumstances. There is far too much latitude involved.
If I appeared before the board as an employee, and if I were to show that I complied with the employment requirements of the act, that I was employed for the appropriate length of time to qualify for benefit but that as a result of having been disabled, ill or laid off, in a technical sense, the time of my employment would be reduced to a point where I might otherwise not be eligible; if the board, having heard my argument, were to accept that I was legitimately laid off, ill, disentitled by way of injury or for any other good reason, then it ought not to be a decision of the board whether it may or may not decide to give me the benefit. Surely, having once accepted that I have given justifiable reason and therefore would otherwise be eligible, the board shall grant the entitlement under the bill.
I suggest that it is a simple word change, but if the board were given the authority to make a decision with regard to the evidence I placed before it, there must be a concurrent responsibility on the board to find in my favour, if my argument is sustained, not simply to say in the end, "Yes, we agree with your argument; yes, I think you should be getting the money; however I have decided, since it is discretionary on the part of the board, not to give it".
Can it work the other way?

No, it cannot work the other way. Unfortunately it cannot because the requirement on the employee is to give proof. The trouble is that it indicates that the employee is qualified to receive labour adjustment benefits, if he shows that he is in substantial compliance with the requirement and that he does not meet such requirement by reason only of
illness, disability, lay-off or any other good cause whatsoever. The onus is placed quite squarely on the shoulders of the employee to prove the good cause. Having once proven that, surely the entitlement should be automatic, not discretionary.
I know the minister is both listening and talking at the same time. I realize ministers develop that rather unique talent immediately after being appointed. However, I suggest that this kind of discretion vested in the board can only cause great hardship in the future. It will cause decisions to be made which cannot be used as precedents because the board will always have discretionary power. For example, it is not inconceivable that in one case an employee could argue that he was disabled but in receipt of workmen's compensation benefits and therefore technically still in the employ of the employer. In so doing, if he could prove to the board that he has a period of employment which would otherwise qualify him for entitlement under the act, he could win because the board might, in exercising its jurisdiction, say, "Yes, I accept it and therefore grant the payment". However, another employee appearing before a differently-structured board with different members could not really use that argument to sustain his case, because the discretion is solely the discretion of the board and the board may or may not grant entitlement.
My argument simply is that that is bad legislation. It does not deal adequately with the concerns of the House of Commons. If it is to set out the criterion under which an employee will receive benefits, once the employee has met the criterion, the benefits should be automatic. I see a head or two on the government side of the House nodding in the affirmative. It should not be discretionary on the part of the board.
Therefore, I ask the Minister of Labour if he would accept that very small word change which would clear up the amendment to the satisfaction of the House of Commons and, in addition, would make it much better in terms of dealing with employees in the future. Will the minister accept the change from "may" to shall?

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member was making such kind remarks about the behaviour of the Minister of Labour, he was listening to him as well as to some good advice coming from my colleague, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead).
I agree.

I listened very carefully to the representations made by the hon. member. But I would like to draw to his attention that Clause 12 begins with:
The commission may determine-
And the paragraph carries all subparagraphs further down on the same page. But the major point in reply to the hon. member is that the word "may" following the words "The commission" gives the commission the full scope to carry out an inquiry without being preconditioned in one direction or another. It is good drafting. Clause 12 is carried with the word "may". It is a way of carrying out the principle into the
February 15, 1982

legislation in the interests of all those concerned. Therefore, I cannot accept the hon. member's proposal.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) rising on a point of order?

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of clarification which I think falls within a point of order. I can well understand the meaning of the word "may" in the operative SubClause 1, that "The commission may determine". But when you get down to a clause which deals specifically with a set of circumstances which must be placed before the board, in that set of circumstances the word "may" is not the appropriate operative word. It is quite clear that the clause reads:
The commission may determine that an employee who has been certilied under Section 9 is qualified to receive labour adjustment benefits if
(a) he is a Canadian citizen resident in Canada-
My concern with it is that an employee could meet every single one of those qualifications as set out in Clause 12(l)(a) through (f). Therefore, Clause 12(1 )(a) to (0 could be met in its entirety, except that the employee might not, in the sense that it is set out, be technically employed through that period as a result of illness and whatever else, the other conditions that are set out in the amendment proposed by the minister. It is an amendment, incidentally, which is not one that we find obnoxious or unacceptable. But if you put in two "mays", you are putting those people in double jeopardy. On the one hand, if in the first section the board may find it subject to these conditions and then you go on to say that additional consideration should be given to a specific set of conditions, then 1 would suggest to the commissioner that the appropriate operative word in the second part is "shall". In the First case, I can appreciate that that you must meet all of those conditions. But having met all those conditions and still having a question as to the appropriateness of the acceptability of the length of time of employment, if the employee can prove that he does qualify under all other terms, then the operative word should be "shall" and not "may".

Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with this particular point. I had experience with the workers' compensation act in Alberta several years ago. The interpretation act said that "may" means "shall" and "shall" means "may". In making representations on behalf of an employee, I found that "may" did not mean "shall", and "shall" did not mean "may", when it came to actual administration. The board rejected this particular claim. When 1 wanted to know why, the board said that it had the discretion. I agreed they had the discretion, but the man was injured in industry, and I asked whether they recognized that. The man had a disability. The doctors claimed that and I asked whether the board recognized that. I asked why they denied him the benefits. They answered that they had the discretion because the. act said "may". We fought that and eventually won the case. I would point out to the minister that administrative boards sometimes bring in other factors that are really irrelevant. This man I have in mind was an obnoxious fellow. People did not like him, but that should not deny him the right to
Labour Adjustment Benefits
compensation when he was injured. Therefore, when every condition is met in this particular requirement, surely the board must accept that and pay a claim. Consequently, why does the minister not want to put in the word "shall" and make it mandatory? The words "may" and "shall" do not mean the same thing. "May" is permissive, "shall" is mandatory.
If the individual meets every requirement, then the word should be "shall". Why is the government going to deny the benefit to an employee because of some irrelevant material? That is what we will do if we leave in the word "may" and not put in the word "shall".
I support the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), I want to say that when he makes his comments he is really not aware of the background of this amendment. He did not participate in the committee hearings.
What does that have to do with it?

I would like to point out to him that there is a basic requirement under Clause 12, to which the hon. member referred, that an employee work 1,000 hours during a period of ten years.
[ Translation]
The Eastern Townships Regional Development Council- [English]
-which suggests that this be replaced by the word "average". In other words, an average 1,000 hours per year over the ten years in the case of somebody who is sick, laid off or disabled for a certain period of time.
The minister, to his credit, listened to the representations made by all sides in the committee. He has come up with an excellent amendment, which the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain grudgingly concedes.
What are you talking about?

In this amendment he is giving discretion to the commission to say that notwithstanding the fact that an employee might not have worked 1,000 hours in any one of those years, the commission may determine that the employee is qualified to receive these benefits if he shows that he did not need it because of illness, disability, lay-off or any other good cause whatever. That expression "any other good cause whatever" is extremely broad. I suggest that the word "may" is necessary in order to go along with that broad expression "any other good cause whatever."
The word "may" is extremely fitting when taken in the context of that last phrase.
In addition to that, I would like to point out to the hon. member and to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) that there is a rule in administrative law that a commission that exercises discretion must exercise that discretion reason-

ably. I would suggest that their concerns are entirely unfounded-
Come on.

-that if a person was able to demonstrate that because of illness or disability he was not able to meet that 1,000-hour requirement and if the commission turned him down, he would be able to appeal that decision before an administrative tribunal in this country and that he would win his appeal. Therefore, in light of principles of administrative law-
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.

The hon. member has referred to an alleged duty of reasonableness on the part of administrative tribunals, and to the possibility that an individual affected by an adverse decision of such a tribunal may appeal. Would the hon. member indicate what his authority is for this suggestion that there is a reasonableness requirement on administrative tribunals? Secondly, would he indicate to whom this rather nebulous appeal would take place?
1 would suggest this is not a nebulous principle, it is a firm principle of administrative law.
Established where?
I would suggest further that an appeal against an unreasonable decision could be directed to one of the courts of the land.
Oh, come on. Why do you write ambiguity into the law?
Furthermore, I would suggest that the principles we are trying to ascribe to the Constitution of this country by virtue of the charter of rights-
Oh, oh!
-would tend to enhance such an appeal.

The House earlier gave its consent to a delay by the Chair in ruling on Motion no. 11. It is approaching ten o'clock and perhaps what we might do is to dispose of Motion No. 11 standing in the name of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen).
The Chair has had the benefit of consultation with the Table and examined the provisions of the bill, in particular Clauses 4 through 7. Under those clauses, the Labour Adjustment Review Board is created, the head office established and the powers of the board are set forth. The motion standing in the name of the hon. member for Kootenay West provides, under Clause 8, for a rather considerable extension of the powers of the board and involves, as referred to in the Speaker's tentative
ruling earlier today, a power to investigate the expected social and economic impact of intended termination of employment.
The motion is faithful to that general principle and discharges upon the board various rights that seem to the Chair, after consultation, to be extensively in excess of the rights conferred on the board under the bill proposed by the minister. Accordingly, the Chair finds, after due consideration, the motion goes beyond the scope of the bill and is out of order.
Now, hon. members may wish to continue the debate on Motions Nos. 13 and 14 which are now on the floor, and for that purpose I will recognize the hon. member for Kootenay West.

Mr. Speaker, I could not help being amused, although it is not a laughing matter, at the comments a few moments ago of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Berger). If he or any member of the House were to visit with working people who have ever had contact with, for example, the Workmen's Compensation Board and suggest to them there is a practice in Canadian law that suggests if a question may go this way or that way, that it go in favour of the victim, he would be lucky to simply be laughed out. In fact, he would be lucky to get out with his head. With the possible exception of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, in which very few Canadian workers would suggest that principle is operative, Workmen's Compensation Board is perhaps the most hated establishment in this land, because it is widely believed that its practice is exactly the opposite, in terms of administration, to that which the member suggested a few moments ago.
On the positive side, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the minister and drafters of the amendments for going a long, long way toward meeting the objections and suggestions raised not only by myself but by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), two or three of the Liberal members of the committee, my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay East-Revel-stoke (Mr. Parker), and others.
While the amendments do not directly deal with the question of the 1,000 hours and whether it should be averaged or required, neither does our own amendment, but it does get around the problem of employees who may find themselves laid off or on sick benefits. In that same spirit I would ask the minister once again to consider the proposal put forward by my House leader a few moments ago, that the word "shall" replace the word "may" in order to make it operative.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia), Mr. Speaker, is new in that position. This is the first bill he has piloted through the House as minister, and he will soon be dealing with major amendments to the Canada Labour Code, both Part IV and Part V, and it will be necessary for him to have the understanding and sympathy of working people across the country in order to help resolve some of the conflicts which happen in labour relations from time to time. Almost everyone, especially blue collar workers, has had experience with grievance procedures, with the law and with commissions, which is perfectly in line with the principles of British common law that property
February 15, 1982

rights always take precedence over human rights unless the law is so clear and so exact that there is no room for anyone to rule in favour of property and against the individual. Unless it is crystal clear, then the worker will believe, as his experience dictates, that he will lose because that is the principle upon which our laws have been based. Hopefully, our charter of rights will start us in slightly another direction in order to balance the ledger. However, it is vitally important for the minister, in order to have credibility with the labour force, to make it clear that he understands that attitude and feeling which exists amongst hundreds of thousands of people in the Canadian work force.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I am not hung up on wording, and the minister has shown before that neither is he if we believe we can solve the problem. With the exception of that one little word I quite agree that the wording as presented by the government is preferable to that submitted by my own party. However, it is important to make it crystal clear to those administering this law that they should follow the intent, and if people are in fact absent and short of that 1,000 hours by virtue of sickness, injury, disability, any good cause whatesoever, they shall be considered to have worked that
1,000	hours, if that is the reason they are short, and be provided with the benefits which this bill provides.
I will conclude with one last and recent example, Mr. Speaker. Just this past year there was a clause in the Canada Labour Code which said in effect-and said it much more clearly than this bill-that if a supervisor refused to work simply because he refused to cross a picket line, he could not be disciplined or lose his job because of that. The Canada Labour Code was crystal clear and it took many months to get justice for those who had lost their jobs, their income, and had their lives disrupted. That was crystal clear. We hope that people in this unfortunate situation will not have to suffer those kinds of delays because of pride and one little word.
Ten o'clock.

subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS-RECEPTION OF TELEVISION SIGNALS FROM CANCOM SATELLITE
COMMUNICATIONS-RECEPTION OF TELEVISION SIGNALS FROM CANCOM SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 24, I put a question to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) concerning the reception of American satellite television signals by local cable television systems in northern Canada. A number of applications are before the Canadian Radio-Television and Telecommunications Commission at the present time to provide local cable television service to many northern communities using the CanCom satellite. The unfortunate part of that whole system is that only four Canadian independent television stations will be received on that system.
My question to the minister was to inquire whether those local cable television systems being established in many northern communities will be able to continue to receive the signals from the American TV satellites, such as the superstations in Chicago and Atlanta and the home box office TV stations.
My reason for putting this question to the minister is that a number of communities in northern Canada have been receiving these American satellite signals in the past, and they have established a cable system and are distributing them to Canadian viewers. Most of them have not been prosecuted in the past, and of course it would be ridiculous for the government to move and do that at the present time, when these communities have no other television available to them. 1 think the problem will be that when these applications which are before the CRTC at the present time are reviewed, we will find that the installation charge and the monthly service fee will be so high that, without the additional American stations being provided to this cable system, they just will not be able to make a go of it.
It seems to me that if the minister does not change the policy and clarify it in the very near future, there will simply be rank discrimination against the northern communities.
We now have the policy in southern Canada for all of the major cities such as Ottawa, Montreal, Toronto, Hamilton, Vancouver and so on, under which they are allowed to receive the three American networks plus the PBS system from the United States on the three plus one formula; but in northern Canada, there is no such provision. There could be rank discrimination against the cable operators in the northern communities and, beyond that, this would just make the situation impossible for most of these cable operators who have applied to have a package which is appealing enough to sell to these small communities. For instance, there are applications before the CRTC for four communities along the north shore of Lake Huron; that is, Iron Bridge, Spanish, Massey and Nairn Centre. The Northern Cable Services is requiring an installation fee of $200, and a monthly service charge of $15 per month. That will not provide any American channels, whereas, in the south, most cable operators provide the three plus one formula.
I hope the minister will clarify this arrangement and provide the same kind of service to northern communities; that is.

American stations as well as the Canadian independents that are on the CanCom satellite. He should rectify this situation which is wholly unfair and, in my view, not workable as it is now established. I hope the parliamentary secretary who responds tonight will state that the government will be able to remove this impediment to the provision of much better television service to many of the communities in northern Ontario and many other northern areas of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: COMMUNICATIONS-RECEPTION OF TELEVISION SIGNALS FROM CANCOM SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question raised by the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), I would like to explain the international understandings which have a bearing on the direct reception in Canada of television signals from U.S. domestic communications satellites.
Both Canada and the United States, as members of the International Telecommunications Satellite Organization, are obliged to consult with IntelSat if they should wish to use their domestic satellite systems to carry communications traffic to or from points in the other country. The two countries would have to demonstrate that any use of non-IntelSat facilities for international telecommunications services would not cause significant economic harm to the IntelSat global satellite system which was established specifically to carry international traffic.
The other arrangement is the 1972 exchange of letters between Canada and the United States under which the two countries have agreed to restrict the use of their domestic satellites for traffic between the two countries only to special circumstances, such as a major technical failure or a temporary shortage of domestic satellite facilities.
It should be noted that all current Canadian and U.S. commercial satellites are classified under regulations of the International Telecommunications Union as constituting fixed satellite services in which radio communication is carried between earth stations at specific fixed points. These are not broadcasting satellites which by definition carry signals intended for direct reception by the general public.
However, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) has made it clear on several occasions that the federal government's major concern is to solve the underlying problem which is giving rise to the unauthorized reception in Canada of U.S. satellite TV signals.
Over the last year very substantial progress has been made in developing a multichannel television service on our ANIK satellite system to meet the basic viewing needs of rural and remote residents who lack the access to television that most Canadians take for granted. Of course, I am referring to CanCom.
CanCom offers a very wide variety of North American programming, both Canadian and U.S. Concerning the wider question of access to U.S. channels, the minister has indicated in the House that it is in the interest of all Canadians that there should be an equalization of viewing opportunities across the country. CanCom is only the first step in this process. The minister has received many requests to open negotiations with
the United States to allow reception of certain U.S. signals in rural and remote communities. This matter is being given very careful consideration within the context of an over-all broadcast strategy currently being developed by the federal government. The objective of the government is definitely to improve service for underserved Canadians in a way that contributes to a healthy environment for the future of the Canadian broadcasting system and serves those communities best.

subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-(A) FORCED IMPLEMENTATION (B) PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS
METRIC CONVERSION-(A) FORCED IMPLEMENTATION (B) PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to bring to the attention of this House and the people of Canada that they are being misled by the government in many of the statements pertaining to the implementation of metric in the retail food stores of this nation.
First, I would like to point out that the acting executive director of the Metric Commission has made the statement over national television that no stores in Peterborough were closed while it was a pilot centre during the implementation of metric. That is clearly not the case. Stores were forced out of business because they would not buy metric weigh scales.
Second, I would like to point out that it has been circulated through the Metric Commission, with the knowledge of the ministry, that 68 per cent of the Canadian people support the implementation of metric in the retail food stores. That is clearly not the case. Ministers also go to press conferences and say that the majority of Canadians support metric. We know from a Gallup poll which was taken in November of 1981, which the same Metric Commission is suppressing, that the majority of Canadians are opposed to forced metric in the retail food stores. This Gallup poll which came to my attention clearly documents that fact.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), who is also the minister responsible for the Metric Commission, when asked a question on January 14, 1981, if there would be fines, confiscation of equipment and imprisonment, answered, as reported in Hansard of January 14, 1981:
we shall not resort to the methods the hon. member would have us use.
In other words, there would be no fines, no confiscation of equipment and no imprisonment. Later I will go on to prove that that is not the case as it applies today.
On April 23, 1980, I asked the same question of the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe); if he intended to sit idly by while the government forced metrication on the people of Canada. The minister replied as reported in Hansard on April 23, 1980 that:
The government has no intention of imposing the metric system manu militari and that it has always been the policy of the Liberal party and government of taking care of the people first, not regulations.
To put the record straight, I would point out an article that appeared in The Calgary Herald. The headline read, "Merchants given metric warning". The article quoted an official of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in Calgary as saying:
February 15, 1982

"We won't come down like a ton of bricks on the first day (but) there might be a couple of prosecutions to wake people up," said Mac Cooper, Calgary operations supervisor for the federal Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, Weights and Measures.
I would like to read from the Winnipeg Free Press dated January 9, 1982. the headline on the editorial page read, "Misleading on metric". The article went on to say:
The Metric Commission, with the backing of the federal government has the unquestioned power to dictate to Canadians that they will henceforth measure their groceries in kilograms rather than in pounds.
Moving on to The Globe and Mail of February 4, 1982, the headline read, "Civil Servant is suspended after protest". Imagine, Mr. Speaker; a civil servant who spoke out against metric in the city of Kingston lost four days pay and an additional ten days pay because he persisted in the principle of freedom of speech and spoke out against forced metric in the city of Kingston.
Let us review some of the businesses. In Kamloops, British Columbia, Gary Cooper said that it will cost him $60,000 to convert the scales in his six stores in British Columbia. An article in the Kamloops News dated December 9, 1981, quoted Cooper as saying:
"There's no turning back now because we're talking about the law ol' the land"
The article went on:
Cooper said metrication is always something that is imposed from above. "Even Napoleon was unable to gel his people to accept metric. He had to impose it."
Another article appearing in the Hamilton Spectator referred to the forced implementation of metric. This particular grocer had been in business for many years. The article stated:
But now, with no sign of reprieve and only weeks remaining before metric conversion becomes law, the aging couple stands a millimetre away from closing their store.
Another article describes a merchant who was willing to face jail. Mac Tackaberry in Kingston is determined he will not be bullied by the federal government and he is prepared to pay the $1,000 fine if necessary and serve the jail sentence that goes along with it. At least there are people in Canada who feel this issue needs full parliamentary debate and should not be handled through regulations that are passed through an order in council without the opportunity for Members of Parliament to debate this method of implementation.
An article appeared in the Daily Mercury dated January 21, 1981, with respect to a merchant in Fergus, Ontario, under the headline "Metric conversion forces retailer to close his doors early". The article states in part:
The move to metric will force a local meat market out of business.
We in the city of Peterborough have lost our only independent dairy. It employed some 40 people. It has been in business for 67 years. The proprietors said:
Adjournment Debate
We invested in the future of our dairy until the metric system came into effect. This made our equipment obsolete, our cartons and glass bottles were no longer of any use.
As of March 1, 1980, when metric was forced on the city of Peterborough this dairy closed its doors and is no longer in business. This was a small family business. The letter from which I have just read was signed by Harold Moncrief, John Moncrief and Gord Moncrief of Moncrief Dairy.
I am a little tired of the government telling the people of Canada that there shall be no force. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has made that statement, as has the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism.
When will this government start telling the people of Canada the truth? There is no voluntary movement to metric in the grocery stores of this nation. This is forced metric against the will of the people, and it is forced without a consensus of Parliament and contrary to the wishes of the people. If the government would release the secret Gallup poll taken for the government in November of 1981, we would see that the poll clearly documented that the people of Canada do not wish metric. Why is that the case? They do not wish metric because they do not wish it by force. They do not mind it by choice, but there is a great difference in metric by force and metric by the choice of the people.
The United States has decided not to force metric on the people of the United States. The Americans have abandoned their metric board. They fired all its members by act of Congress to be effective September, 1982. Britain is totally back to miles an hour on the highway and pounds in the grocery store. The British are back to Fahrenheit at the weather bureaus of their nation. Let us not have any of this nonsense about the whole world going metric. The fact of the matter is that the whole world is not going metric, unless by choice.
Only Canada is going metric. Canada is a free country-we think-but the people have lost the right to choose. The Metric Commission is dictating to the Government of Canada the implementation time-frame against the will of the people and without a consensus, and the government will not even release the results of a Gallup pool paid for by the people of Canada which indicated that the people do not wish metric at this time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gary F. McCauley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-(A) FORCED IMPLEMENTATION (B) PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like very briefly once again to address the concerns of the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) with regard to the enforcement of regulations made under the Weights and Measures Act for metric conversion of individually measured foods and scale conversion.
As the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) has already informed the hon. member, the enforcement of these regulations will be conducted in a decent and appropriate manner, and we shall not resort to the methods the hon. member has suggested at various and sundry times in the House.

February 15, 1982
Adjournment Debate
I can tell the hon. member that it will be the responsibility of Consumer and Corporate Affairs Canada to enforce regulations made under the Weights and Measures Act in exactly the same manner as all other such regulations are enforced.
Our well-established inspection practice in all instances involves first informing non-complying retailers of their obligations under the law, in this case to advertise and sell individually-measured foods as required by these regulations. Then we encourage the retailers to take whatever action is necessary to comply with the regulations. Should a retailer not take action to comply with the regulations, then he would be advised in writing that continued non-compliance would result in the initiation of prosecution action.

subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-(A) FORCED IMPLEMENTATION (B) PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS
speechtext: That is force.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: METRIC CONVERSION-(A) FORCED IMPLEMENTATION (B) PRIME MINISTER'S VIEWS
speechtext:
Should a retailer be prosecuted for noncompliance with these regulations, I might point out that the highest penalty that could be imposed in such cases would be a maximum fine of $1,000 for each offence. I might also point out that devices would only be seized in those instances where that would be required in the gathering of evidence for enforcement action.
I would also like to assure the hon. member that we do not anticipate that extensive enforcement action will be required to ensure compliance with these regulations. Unlike him, we have every confidence that retailers of individually measured foods will convert to metric as required. Surely, the hon. member realizes that Canadian retailers are good corporate citizens who will obey the law.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-CALLING OF TENDERS FOR ADVERTISING CONCESSION
AIRPORTS-CALLING OF TENDERS FOR ADVERTISING CONCESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fair and proper tendering procedures are very important in this country, not only to the government but to business and consumers. On December 17 when I raised with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) the issue of the failure to institute proper or any tendering procedures for advertising in airports, he gave me an answer which I thought was rather unsatisfactory. We spoke about tendering for advertising concessions and in the course of our dialogue we also discussed duty-free procedures which are obviously very important in terms of the policy of the department.
There are many incongruities here, Mr. Speaker. I will deal first with the specific question of the Toronto International Airport where over $200,000 per month was lost for two and a half years because FIRA-the misbegotten agency of federal government which has done so much to discourage investment in this country-took that long to decide what should be done with the people who were awarded the duty-free franchise at that airport.
Finally, in disgust, I understand, Duty Free Shopping Group Ltd. of Honolulu, threw up its hands because of the delays. That is amazing when one realizes that Mr. Robert Campeau's organization was able to sell the Harbour Castle Hotel to
Hong Kong interests in ten days. It would be nice if FIRA and the Department of Transport got together and did something even remotely like that to settle the duty-free agency at the Toronto International Airport. If they had, they could have saved the taxpayers over $5 million. I suppose it depends on who you are.
Since the minister raised the issue of Sky Shops, I want to refer to what is going on at Dorval Airport. As I understand it, it is long-standing department policy that when someone tenders for a concession-in this case a duty-free one in the Dorval Airport-it is enforced by the Department of Transport. The company is then supposed to pay the greater of a minimum guarantee or of a percentage of sales. I understand that business is such that this is not being done; the company is merely paying a percentage of sales, which is less than the minimum guarantee. Obviously, that particular concession to Thomcor should be terminated. That company is the successor to Sky Shops which, as a matter of passing interest, Mr. Speaker, once sued me for $500,000 for pointing out that one could buy things cheaper on the street than in their duty-free shops. They were pleased to withdraw that suit, with costs. That is in the past, however.
I want to point out again that there is something very wrong in the administration of the Department of Transport. 1 want to know who authorized this departure from departmental policy whereby a contract, which is tendered on the basis of payment of either the greater of the minimum guarantee or the percentage of sales, is wilfully disregarded. 1 believe that is also true of the Quebec restaurants and probably of other concessions as well.
If the parliamentary secretary does not have an answer for me tonight, I hope he can find out who authorized this departure from a clearly set out policy designed for the benefit of consumers and in the interests of fairness to the people who tender.
On the subject of Dorval, I have a very great interest in seeing that the concessions in that airport are operating in a healthy and respectable state and, indeed, that the airport is maintained in its present condition. I think it would be a travesty to close this well-used and successful airport, which is making money, for the sake of transferring a lot of these operations to that white elephant, Mirabel, which is costing the Canadian taxpayer about $1 million per month in operational cost deficits alone. But I am wandering off the subject and I apologize for that.
1 should like to ask my hon. friend opposite if he can assure me tonight that the government and the Department of Transport will get off their proverbial seats and do something about getting a proper tendering procedure instituted for airport advertising. At the same time, they should take a hard look at what is going on in terms of altering-unilaterally, I suspect- a policy that is very clearly understood and is designed to bring in revenue and ensure fairness when it comes to honouring the contracts awarded by tender. There may be good reason why the Thomcor company cannot pay-perhaps business is bad. If it is an impoverished organization, it is clear the contract
February 15, 1982

should be revoked and that the concession should be awarded to the next highest bidder or, failing that, it should be retendered. But allowing these irregularities to perpetuate themselves, in defiance of fairness and established policy, does not do the government, the Department of Transport or the Canadian public any good. 1 would urge the minister to take a very close look at these procedures and report to the House as soon as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS-CALLING OF TENDERS FOR ADVERTISING CONCESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the information of the hon. member, Duty Free Shops Limited definitely decided not to take up its contract. The present concessionaire is to continue on an interim basis until a new concessionaire is selected by a new tender call which is expected to be placed in the very near future.
Prior to 1969, very little advertising was sold at airports, revenues were minimal, and there were no standards regarding size and quality of displays or rates to be charged for advertising space. Because the department had very little background in advertising, it was decided to develop this medium through the expertise of an advertising concessionaire. In 1969, the Department of Transport called for tenders for the right to sell advertising at ten Canadian airports.
Adjournment Debate
The concessionaire began operating on January 1, 1970, with a Five-year agreement which was renewable for a further Five years. The renewal was granted in 1975. During the term of the agreement, the concessionaire was granted additional rights to sell advertising at smaller airports, if he could show that the revenues generated by the company exceeded those which could have been achieved by the department. Within the ten-year period, from 1970 to 1980, the company sold advertising at 13 additional airports in Canada. The company has been granted two extensions of short duration to the original contract. The second extension expires on June 30 of this year. The main reason for the extension was to permit the Department of Transport time to develop linguistic requirements for advertising at airports and to include these requirements in the speciFications for the next tender call.
Linguistic requirements have been completed and a public tender for the concessionaire will be announced in the newspapers on February 26 and February 27, 1982. We expect the award to be determined on or about May 1.
